basic_identification.name: Attention economy critique in digital art
basic_identification.originator: Theoretical: Jonathan Crary (24/7: Late Capitalism and the Ends of Sleep), Tim Wu (The Attention Merchants), Herbert Simon (original attention scarcity concept). Digital art context: Xiaonan Qi (Algorithmic Gatekeepers, SSRN 2025), Brooke Erin Duffy and Colten Meisner (Platform governance at the margins, 2023), Georgetown Law Denny Center (Cognitive Autonomy). Art criticism: TDR/Cambridge Core (The Work of Art in the Age of Digital Commodification, 2024). Practitioners raising concern: artists experiencing algorithmic invisibility, burnout, and platform dependency.
basic_identification.geography: Global discourse, primarily articulated in US and EU academic and art criticism contexts. Platform dynamics are global but uneven: Instagram/Meta dominant in Western markets, TikTok globally, WeChat/Weibo in China.

core_ideas.core_claim: Digital art practice has become structurally dependent on platform attention economies that treat artistic content as engagement fuel rather than cultural expression. Algorithms determine visibility, discovery operates through engagement metrics rather than curatorial judgment, and artists are forced to optimize for platform logic rather than artistic intention. Artistic content is subsumed by commodity logic, appearing alongside all other content and competing on engagement metrics. Platform disintermediation promised democratization but delivered reintermediation through algorithmic systems that rank content based on profit potential.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Unique to digital art in its mechanism: physical art galleries select through human curation, while digital art visibility is algorithmically determined. The engagement metrics that drive visibility (likes, shares, time-on-screen, saves) measure attention capture rather than artistic significance. Digital art is uniquely vulnerable because it exists natively within the platforms that commodify it. A painting in a gallery is not in competition with all other content; a digital artwork on Instagram is.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: This IS the attention economy critique applied to digital art. The core analysis: platform algorithms extract attention from viewers and convert it into advertising revenue, using artistic content as engagement bait. Artists become unpaid content producers for platforms. Visibility is a function of engagement optimization, not artistic quality. Marginalized artists face compounded invisibility as algorithms replicate offline biases. The attention economy creates winner-takes-most dynamics where a small number of viral artists receive disproportionate visibility while the majority are invisible.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: The critique identifies a fundamental conflict between attention-native platform logic and intention-native artistic practice. Platforms optimize for engagement (attention); artists declare needs for fair visibility, meaningful curation, and sustainable practice (intention). The critique argues that current infrastructure is structurally incapable of serving artistic intention because it is designed to capture attention. Alternative discovery infrastructure serving intention rather than attention is the core demand.

market_economics.revenue_model: The attention economy model: platforms are free to use, funded by advertising revenue extracted from user attention. Artists provide content that attracts viewers whose attention is sold to advertisers. Artists receive visibility (not money) in exchange for content. Some platforms offer creator funds (TikTok, Instagram bonuses) but these are minor relative to advertising revenue. The economic model is: artists subsidize platforms with free content in exchange for algorithmically rationed visibility.
market_economics.market_position: The attention economy critique positions platforms as exploitative intermediaries between artists and audiences. Platforms capture the value created by artistic content (attention/engagement) and monetize it through advertising. Artists receive exposure rather than compensation. The market position is parasitic: platforms extract value from creative labor without adequate compensation.
market_economics.price_range: Not directly applicable. The attention economy does not price art; it prices attention. CPM (cost per thousand impressions) on Instagram ranges from $2-$12. An artist's work generates value for the platform measured in ad revenue, not art market prices. The disconnect between attention value (measured in impressions) and art value (measured in aesthetic/cultural significance) is the core structural problem.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Platform dependency intensifying. Meta is integrating AI chatbots into discovery, making algorithmic mediation even more opaque. Instagram and TikTok remain dominant discovery platforms for digital art. Artist engagement with platforms shows no decline despite widespread dissatisfaction. The trend is increasing dependency with increasing critique - a structural trap. Alternative platforms (Cara, founded by artists for artists) gaining traction but remain marginal. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: 35% of millennial collectors rely exclusively on social media for art discovery. Younger collectors are less reliant on galleries and fairs, more dependent on algorithmic discovery. This means collector demographics are increasingly shaped by platform algorithms rather than curatorial expertise. Collectors who rely on social media encounter a algorithmically-curated subset of available art rather than the full field. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: The platform attention economy is commercially sustainable for platforms (multi-billion dollar businesses) but unsustainable for artists (burnout, precarity, creative compromise). Making a living as an artist got harder in 2025. Some artists leaving the industry entirely. Others learning new tools or returning to traditional media as an antidote. The sustainability crisis is for practitioners, not platforms.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Artists use: Instagram, TikTok, X/Twitter, Bluesky, Discord for visibility. Portfolio platforms: ArtStation, Behance, personal websites. Alternative platforms: Cara (artist-focused, no AI training), FOLLOW.ART. Content optimization tools: scheduling apps, analytics dashboards, hashtag research. The toolchain includes both art-making tools and visibility-optimization tools, with the latter consuming increasing time and attention.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: AI compounds the attention economy problem in two ways: (1) generative AI floods platforms with content, increasing competition for attention and devaluing human-made art; (2) AI-powered algorithms become more sophisticated in attention capture, making platform logic more opaque. Meta's AI chatbot integration into search and discovery means artists must optimize for AI interpretation, not human curation. The framing shifts from artist-to-audience communication to artist-to-algorithm communication.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: The attention economy demands constant liveness: regular posting, real-time engagement, story updates, live streams. Algorithmic visibility rewards recency and consistency over quality or depth. Artists who take breaks lose algorithmic visibility. This creates a performative liveness divorced from artistic liveness - the constant performance of being an active creator rather than the genuine liveness of evolving artistic practice.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Algorithmic visibility, engagement metrics, content optimization, shadow ban, algorithmic bias, platform dependency, creator economy, attention extraction, cognitive autonomy, digital anxiety, identity fragmentation, self-curation, performative relevance. The vocabulary is emerging at the intersection of media studies, platform criticism, and art discourse. It lacks adequate terms for describing what art would look like if freed from attention optimization.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: The attention economy is: enclosure (platforms enclose the attention commons), capture (extracting value from creative labor), spectacle (optimizing for visual impact over structural substance), and individualistic (rewarding personal brand over collective practice). The critique itself tends toward: openness (public discourse), commons (shared analytical framework), infrastructure (proposing systemic alternatives), and collective (identifying structural rather than individual problems).

infrastructure_governance.openness: Platforms are proprietary and opaque. Algorithmic logic is not disclosed. Content moderation rules are unevenly applied. Shadow banning operates without notification. The attention economy is built on proprietary, closed infrastructure that artists cannot inspect, modify, or meaningfully contest. The critique demands transparency that platforms resist because opacity enables attention extraction.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Corporate governance with no artist representation. Platform decisions about algorithmic ranking, content moderation, and feature design are made by technology companies with no accountability to artist communities. Creator advisory boards exist at some platforms but have no binding authority. The governance model is autocratic from the artist's perspective.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Artists do not own their audience relationships on platforms. Follower lists, engagement data, and algorithmic reach are platform-controlled. Artists cannot export their audience. Platform changes (algorithm updates, policy changes, service termination) can destroy years of audience-building overnight. Data sovereignty is almost entirely absent for artists on social media platforms.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Very low. Each platform is a walled garden. Followers on Instagram do not transfer to TikTok. Content formats are platform-specific. Cross-posting degrades content (Instagram deprioritizes content with TikTok watermarks). No standard protocol for artist identity or audience portability across platforms. ActivityPub (Mastodon, Threads partially) is the only interoperability standard gaining traction.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Platform content is ephemeral by design. Stories disappear after 24 hours. Algorithm changes bury older content. Platforms can delete content or suspend accounts without notice. No platform provides adequate archival or export tools. Artist content on platforms has no preservation guarantee. The attention economy is structurally opposed to preservation - it requires novelty, not permanence.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Deeply problematic. Artists consent to platform terms of service (often granting broad content licenses) in exchange for visibility. Viewers consent to attention extraction through continued use. Neither consent is meaningfully informed. The attention economy operates through what Georgetown Law calls attentional intrusion - the exploitation of mental space without meaningful consent. Cookie consent mechanisms are superficial. No consent architecture exists for algorithmic attention capture.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: The attention economy critique applies differently to traditional and digital art. Traditional art world maintains human-curated discovery (galleries, fairs, studio visits) alongside platform-mediated visibility. Digital art is more deeply embedded in platform logic. However, the traditional art world increasingly uses social media for discovery and promotion. A 2025 study found that platforms have disintermediated markets for books, film, and music, but the online art market reproduced offline structures, leaving traditional intermediaries intact.
field_position.what_it_enables: Critical awareness of structural forces shaping art practice. Identification of specific mechanisms of attention capture. Framework for evaluating alternative discovery infrastructure. Language for artists to articulate their experience of platform dependency. Political demand for algorithmic transparency and artist data rights. Foundation for building attention-resistant art infrastructure.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Viable alternatives at scale. Most critique identifies the problem without providing functional replacements for platform-mediated discovery. No attention-economy-resistant art platform has achieved mass adoption. The critique lacks: concrete infrastructure proposals, economic models for attention-free art discovery, and transition pathways for artists currently dependent on platforms. The field can name the problem but has not built the alternative.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Artists from marginalized identities face compounded algorithmic invisibility - platform governance enacted unevenly through shadow bans and biased algorithmic boosts. Artists who refuse platform participation become invisible to a generation of collectors who discover exclusively through social media. Artists without digital literacy or internet access. Older artists unfamiliar with platform optimization. Artists whose work does not translate to screen-based, scroll-optimized formats. Artists in regions with restricted platform access.
field_position.frontier_signal: Established critique with frontier implications. The problem is well-diagnosed. The frontier: building functional alternatives. Emerging efforts include Cara, FOLLOW.ART, Farcaster (decentralized social), and protocol-based social media (ActivityPub). AI integration into discovery (Meta's AI chatbot) represents a new frontier where the problem intensifies rather than resolves.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: The attention economy critique is discovered through: academic publication, art press (Artnet, Artsy, Creative Bloq, Art Review), social media discussion (ironic, given the critique), conference presentations, and word of mouth within artist communities. The critique circulates within the system it critiques, creating a recursive dynamic: attention to the attention economy critique is itself mediated by attention economy platforms.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: The critique itself has moderate attention dependency - it needs visibility to be effective. However, the structural analysis becomes embedded in academic and institutional discourse that persists independently of social media attention. The long-form academic versions (Duffy & Meisner, Cambridge Core, Georgetown Law) have low attention dependency. The popular versions (Medium posts, Twitter threads) have high attention dependency.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: The critique is the most intention-aligned discourse in the field: it explicitly names the conflict between attention capture and artistic intention and demands infrastructure that serves intention. It articulates the structural need that the field has declared but cannot meet: discovery mechanisms based on artistic significance rather than engagement metrics. The critique is intention-native analysis of an attention-native system.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Significant theoretical commons contribution. The analytical framework is publicly available through academic publications and open discourse. However, the critique has not yet produced commons infrastructure (no open-source alternative discovery platform at scale). The contribution is conceptual rather than operational: the field has a shared diagnosis but not a shared treatment.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Meaning provenance: the critique tracks how attention dynamics shape the meaning and reception of art, not ownership. It provides context for understanding why certain artists are visible and others are not - a form of provenance that explains absence as well as presence.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Real-time and cyclical. Platform algorithms operate in real-time, constantly reshuffling visibility. Artist attention is captured in perpetual present-tense engagement cycles. The critique itself operates in academic-time (annual publication cycles) and social-media-time (viral moments of collective frustration). The temporal conflict is between the platform's demand for perpetual present-tense engagement and the artistic need for deep, non-urgent time.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The critique centrally addresses absence: algorithmically invisible artists, shadow-banned content, excluded demographics, and the structural absence of alternative discovery mechanisms. This is one of the few discourses in digital art that explicitly accounts for what is not visible rather than only what is. The attention economy creates systematic absence that the critique makes visible.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Broad coherence that platform attention economies are problematic for art. No consensus on solutions: some advocate regulation, others decentralized alternatives, others platform reform, others exit from platforms entirely. The critique accommodates multiple valid perspectives on the problem and its solutions without requiring agreement. Coherence without consensus.
coherence.contestability: The factual basis (platform algorithms determine visibility, engagement metrics shape practice) is broadly uncontested. Platform companies contest the characterization of their systems as exploitative. Some artists contest the critique by arguing that platforms provide genuine opportunities for visibility that would not otherwise exist. The critique is contested at the normative level (is this bad?) rather than the descriptive level (is this happening?).
coherence.forkability: The analytical framework is freely forkable: anyone can apply attention economy analysis to their context. Alternative platform projects (Cara, Farcaster, FOLLOW.ART) represent forks of the solution space. The critique is modular and adaptable to different cultural contexts. However, the problem itself cannot be forked away - it is structural to commercial platform design.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The attention/intention distinction as a core analytical framework. The critique of engagement metrics as false signals of significance. The demand for discovery mechanisms based on structural relevance rather than algorithmic popularity. The analysis of how platform design shapes what gets made and who gets seen. The emphasis on absence-detection: what the attention economy makes invisible is as important as what it surfaces.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The purely critical posture that diagnoses without building. A(DAI) must not only critique the attention economy but construct intention-native alternatives. Refuse the recursive trap of using attention economy platforms to critique the attention economy without building functional alternatives. Refuse engagement metrics as inputs to the knowledge graph. Refuse the assumption that visibility equals significance.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: A(DAI) aims to be an intention-native alternative to attention-economy art infrastructure. But A(DAI) itself needs attention to gain adoption and participation. The tension: how to build intention-native infrastructure that people can discover without relying on attention-native platforms for discovery. A(DAI) must solve the bootstrapping problem - creating an alternative discovery mechanism that can become visible without becoming attention-dependent.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: EU Digital Services Act (DSA) requires platform transparency about algorithmic systems. EU AI Act may classify recommendation algorithms as high-risk AI systems, requiring auditing. California AB 587 requires social media companies to publish content moderation policies. Georgetown Law advocates for legal recognition of attentional intrusion. No specific regulation protects artists from algorithmic invisibility, but general platform regulation is evolving.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Platform terms of service typically grant broad content licenses. Instagram's terms grant a non-exclusive, royalty-free, transferable, sub-licensable, worldwide license to use content. Artists retain copyright but grant platforms extensive usage rights through consent to terms of service. The IP model is technically artist-owned but practically platform-licensed.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Platform participation is opt-in but practically required for artist visibility. Opting out means becoming invisible to a generation of collectors and curators. Algorithmic attention capture is opt-out impossible - you cannot use the platform without being subject to its algorithms. Cookie consent and privacy settings provide superficial opt-out for some data collection but not for the fundamental attention capture mechanism.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Extremely high. Instagram, TikTok, X/Twitter, and Discord are the primary discovery infrastructure for digital art. No viable alternative exists at comparable scale. Platform changes (algorithm updates, feature changes, policy shifts) directly impact artist livelihoods and visibility. Single point of failure risk: if Instagram's algorithm deprioritizes art content (as it has periodically), the entire art discovery ecosystem is disrupted.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong winner-takes-most network effects favor dominant platforms. Instagram's billion-plus users create a discovery advantage that no alternative can match. Network effects lock artists in: leaving means losing accumulated followers and algorithmic standing. The critique identifies network effects as the structural barrier to alternatives - artists cannot leave because their audience cannot leave.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The attention economy critique has intensified post-NFT-crash. With market speculation declining, platform visibility became even more important for digital artists seeking alternative revenue. AI integration into platform discovery (Meta AI chatbot, 2025-2026) represents a new escalation. The trajectory is deepening dependency with deepening critique - the problem is growing rather than resolving. Alternative platforms remain marginal.
